claim: Early-life stress can have lifelong consequences, enhancing stress susceptibility and resulting in behavioural and cognitive deficits.
source_text: Early-life stress can have lifelong consequences, enhancing stress susceptibility and resulting in behavioural and cognitive deficits.
evidence_reasoning: This statement draws from established scientific consensus about early-life stress effects and is supported by citations in the manuscript (Walker et al., 2017; Joëls and Baram, 2009; Lopez and Bagot, 2021; O'Donnell and Meaney, 2020; Meaney, 2001).

claim: Early-life stress induces anxiety-like behaviour and fear generalisation in an amygdala-dependent learning and memory task in male and female mice.
source_text: Here, using male and female mice we report that early-life stress induces anxiety-like behaviour and fear generalisation in an amygdala-dependent learning and memory task.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including behavioral assays shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Behavioral changes from early-life stress were associated with impaired synaptic plasticity, increased neural excitability, and astrocyte hypofunction.
source_text: These behavioural changes were associated with impaired synaptic plasticity, increased neural excitability, and astrocyte hypofunction.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental measurements including electrophysiology data (Figure 2G-H), c-Fos labeling (Figure 2J-L), and calcium imaging (Figure 4).

claim: Genetic perturbation of amygdala astrocyte function by reducing astrocyte calcium activity or reducing astrocyte network function was sufficient to replicate cellular, synaptic, and fear memory generalisation associated with early-life stress.
source_text: Genetic perturbation of amygdala astrocyte function by either reducing astrocyte calcium activity or reducing astrocyte network function was sufficient to replicate cellular, synaptic, and fear memory generalisation associated with early-life stress.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from viral manipulation experiments shown in Figure 5, including behavioral, electrophysiological, and immunohistochemical measurements.

claim: Early-life stress has widespread effects across the brain and can influence neural circuits involved in threat detection, emotion, cognitive processing, and reward-seeking behaviours.
source_text: Early-life stress (ELS) has widespread effects across the brain and can influence many neural circuits including those involved in threat detection, emotion, cognitive processing, and reward-seeking behaviours
evidence_reasoning: This statement is supported by multiple citations (Peña et al., 2017; Peña et al., 2019; Lesuis et al., 2018; Lesuis et al., 2019) and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Research investigating the neurobiology of stress has predominantly focused upon the effects on neurons and resulting behaviour.
source_text: Research investigating the neurobiology of stress has predominantly focused upon the effects on neurons and resulting behaviour
evidence_reasoning: This is a characterization of the field supported by multiple citations and reflects established scientific consensus about research trends.
